title: Proof By Contradiction
body:
Assume the claim is **false**, and derive something impossible. Since the reasoning was
valid and the conclusion is false, the assumption must have been the problem, so the claim
is true.

This is the technique for claims that assert a negative: "there is no such thing", "this
language is not regular", "$\sqrt{2}$ is not rational". A [[Direct Proof]] needs something
to build, and a negative gives you nothing to build with. Assuming the positive, on the
other hand, hands you a concrete object to take apart.

## The shape

```
Claim: P
1. Suppose, for contradiction, that ¬P.
2. ... reasoning, all of it valid ...
3. Therefore Q and ¬Q.          ← the contradiction
4. Step 1 is the only thing that could be wrong, so P.  ∎
```

The contradiction in step 3 does not have to relate to the claim. Anything impossible
works: a number that is both even and odd, a set both empty and non-empty, a machine that
halts exactly when it does not.

## Worked example

```
Claim: √2 is irrational.

Suppose not: √2 = a/b, with a and b integers sharing no common factor
(any fraction can be reduced to this form).

    2 = a²/b²
    a² = 2b²          so a² is even, so a is even
    a = 2c
    4c² = 2b²
    b² = 2c²          so b² is even, so b is even

a and b are both even, so they share the factor 2.
But we chose them with no common factor. Contradiction.
So no such a and b exist, and √2 is irrational.  ∎
```

"$a^2$ is even, so $a$ is even" is itself a small proof, usually done by contraposition
(if $a$ is odd then $a^2$ is odd). Proofs nest.

## Where this is used

This is the workhorse of [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]], and the two arguments the
course is built around are both instances of it:

- The **[[Pumping Lemma]]**: to show a language is not regular, assume it *is*, get the
  pumping length $p$ the lemma promises, pick a string that the lemma's own guarantee
  cannot survive, and pump it out of the language. Every use of the pumping lemma has this
  form, without exception.
- The **halting problem** in [[Turing Machine]] and [[Undecidability]]: assume a decider
  $H$ exists, build a machine that asks $H$ what it will do and then does the opposite, and
  run it on itself. Both answers are wrong, so $H$ does not exist. This one adds
  self-reference and diagonalisation on top of the plain contradiction skeleton.

Both are proofs that something is *impossible*, which is exactly when this technique is
the only one available.

## Contradiction versus contraposition

They are different and get confused constantly.

| | Assume | Prove | Conclude |
|---|---|---|---|
| Contraposition | $\lnot B$ | $\lnot A$ | if $A$ then $B$ |
| Contradiction | $A$ and $\lnot B$ | anything false | if $A$ then $B$ |

Contraposition proves a logically equivalent statement, so the result is a direct proof of
a rearranged claim. Contradiction proves the original claim by eliminating the alternative.
If your contradiction proof never uses the assumption $A$, you actually wrote a
contraposition and it will read more cleanly as one.
